## **Avian Baseline Studies for the North Sky River Wind Energy Project Kern County, California**

**Winter Interim Report May 18, 2010 – February 28, 2011**

## **Prepared for: CH2M HILL**

## **Prepared by:**

**Andrea Chatfield and Kimberly Bay**

Western EcoSystems Technology, Inc. 2003 Central Avenue Cheyenne, Wyoming 82001

## **April 18, 2011**

**NATURAL RESOURCES**  **SCIENTIFIC SOLUTIONS**

_`Draft Pre-Decisional Document - Privileged and Confidential - Not For Distribution`_

## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

Next-Era Energy (Next-Era) is proposing to develop a wind energy facility in Kern County, California, referred to as the North Sky River Wind Energy Project (Project). In May of 2010, Western EcoSystems Technology, Inc. (WEST) initiated surveys and monitoring of wildlife resources for CH2M HILL at the Project. The avian studies implemented during the summer and fall of 2010 and the winter of 2010/2011 are part of a larger 1-year study. Seasonal interim reports are designed to give CH2M HILL an early warning of high wildlife use or if sensitive species are observed within the study area. The scope of the 2010/2011 wildlife studies included fixed-point bird use surveys and acoustic bat surveys. Results of the bat surveys are presented in a separate report.

A total of 721 30-minute (min) fixed-point bird use surveys were conducted within the Project during 41 visits from May 18, 2010 to February 28, 2011. A total of 288 fixed-point surveys were conducted in the summer during 16 visits, 180 surveys were conducted in the fall during 10 visits, and 253 surveys were conducted in the winter during 15 visits. During the surveys, 120 unique bird species were observed, and a total of 12,713 individual bird observations within 4,058 separate groups were recorded.

Passerines were the most abundant bird type recorded, accounting for 71.3% of all observations. This was primarily due to relatively high numbers of horned larks, dark-eyed juncos, white-crowned sparrows, western scrub-jays, and mountain bluebirds observed. These five passerine species represented only 4.2% of all the bird species observed, yet accounted for 42.7% of the total bird observations. Large corvids were the second most abundant bird type observed in the study area, representing 12.0% of all observations, while upland game birds were the third most abundant bird type, accounting for 9.7% of all observations. A total of 269 diurnal raptor observations were made during fixed-point surveys, and 10 separate species were observed. Diurnal raptors accounted for 2.1% of all observations, with red-tailed hawk, American kestrel, and golden eagle being the most commonly observed diurnal raptors.

A comparison of mean raptor use (number of raptors divided by the number of 800-meter [m; 2,625-foot (ft)] plots and the total number of surveys) was made between the Project and other existing and proposed wind energy facilities with similarly collected data. During the summer, fall, and winter observation periods, the adjusted mean raptor use in the Project was considered low (0.25, 0.27, and 0.20 raptors/plot/20-minute survey, respectively) relative to other wind resource areas with data for summer, fall, or winter.

One state-endangered species (willow flycatcher), six state species of special concern (loggerhead shrike, Vaux’s swift, American white pelican, gray vireo, northern harrier, and yellow warbler), and two federal species of concern (loggerhead shrike and ferruginous hawk) were recorded during fixed point surveys or incidentally. Additionally, golden eagles, a species protected under the federal Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and a fully protected species in California, were observed during surveys.

Five sensitive species were observed incidentally at the Project. These included two species not observed during fixed-point bird use surveys: the state-threatened Swainson’s hawk and the state species of special concern, American white pelican. Golden eagle, ferruginous hawk, and northern harrier were also observed incidental to the fixed-point surveys.

## **INTRODUCTION**

Next-Era Energy (Next-Era) is proposing to develop a wind energy facility in Kern County, California, referred to as the North Sky River Wind Energy Project (Project). CH2M HILL, a contractor to Next-Era, requested that Western EcoSystems Technology, Inc. (WEST) develop and implement a standardized protocol for avian baseline studies in the Project with the purpose of estimating impacts of the proposed wind energy facility on avian resources and to assist with siting turbines to minimize impacts. The protocol for the baseline studies is similar to those used at other wind energy facilities across the nation, and follows the guidance of the California Wind Energy Guidelines (CEC and CDFG 2007) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) Wind Turbine Guidelines Advisory Committee (WTGAC 2010). The protocols have been developed based on WEST’s experience studying wildlife at proposed wind energy facilities throughout the US; and were designed to help predict potential impacts to birds (particularly raptors).

The purpose of the following interim report is to bring items of biological interest to CH2M HILL’s attention, such as seasonal and spatial raptor use and the presence of sensitive species. The scope of the summer and fall 2010 and winter 2010/2011 wildlife studies included fixed-point bird use surveys and acoustic bat surveys. Results of the bat surveys are presented in a separate report. This interim report presents preliminary data on number of observations by species and bird type, as well as sensitive species observations and incidental wildlife observations. The final avian report will include results for all data collected.

## **STUDY AREA**

The Project is situated primarily on private land within east-central Kern County (Figure 1). The proposed wind energy facility falls near the intersection of two ecological subsections, the High Desert Plains and Hills Subsection of the Mojave Desert to the south and east, and the Eastern Slopes Subsection of the Sierra Nevada to the north and west (USFS 1997). Topography within the study area is characterized by gently rolling hills to relatively steep, low mountains, and elevations range from approximately 3,120 feet (ft; 950 meters [m]) in the southeastern portion of the Project to just over 5,580 ft (1,700 m) in the southwest. The dominant vegetation community is Mojavean juniper ( _Juniperus_ spp.) woodland and scrub characterized by widely spaced California junipers ( _J. californica_ ) interspersed with smaller woody shrubs, forbs, and grasses. Desert scrub vegetation with small areas of Joshua tree ( _Yucca brevifolia_ ) woodland are present within the lower elevations of the study area, while juniper-pinyon pine ( _Pinus monophylla_ ) and oak ( _Quercus_ spp.) woodlands are found at the higher elevations.

**Figure 1. Study area map and fixed-point bird use observation locations for the North Sky Wind Energy Project.**

Several natural springs occur throughout the study area, as well as a number of small intermittent drainages which contain riparian vegetation such as willow ( _Salix_ spp) and tamarisk ( _Tamarix_ spp). Cottonwood Creek runs through the center of the Project from the northwest to the southeast and contains more substantial riparian woodlands with an overstory comprised primarily of Fremont cottonwood _(Populus fremontii_ ). The Pacific Crest Trail cuts through the southwestern corner of the study area (Figure 1).

## **METHODS**

## **Fixed-Point Bird Use Surveys**

The objective of the fixed-point bird use surveys was to estimate the seasonal and spatial use of the study area by birds, particularly diurnal raptors, defined here as kites, accipiters, buteos, eagles, falcons, and osprey. Fixed-point surveys (variable circular plots) were conducted using methods described by Reynolds et al. (1980).

## _Bird Use Survey Plots_

Eighteen points were selected to survey representative habitats and topography of the study area while also providing relatively even spatial coverage (Figure 1). Each survey plot was an 800-m (2,625-ft) radius circle centered on the point.

## _Bird Survey Methods_

All species of birds observed during each 30-minute (min) fixed-point survey were recorded. Observations of large birds beyond the 800-m radius were recorded, but were not included in the statistical analyses. For small birds, observations beyond a 100-m (328-ft) radius were also excluded from analyses. Large birds included waterbirds, waterfowl, rails/coots, shorebirds, diurnal raptors, owls, vultures, upland game birds, doves/pigeons, large cuckoos (i.e., roadrunners [ _Geococcyx_ spp.]), goatsuckers, and large corvids (e.g., ravens [ _Corvus_ spp.] and magpies [ _Pica_ spp.]). Passerines (excluding large corvids), swifts/hummingbirds, and woodpeckers are considered small birds.

The date, start, and end time of the survey period, and weather information such as temperature, wind speed, wind direction, and cloud cover were recorded for each survey. Species or best possible identification, number of individuals, sex and age class (if possible), distance from plot center when first observed, closest distance, altitude above ground, activity (behavior), and habitat(s) were recorded for each observation. Behavior and habitat type were recorded based on the point of first observation. Approximate flight height and flight direction at first observation were recorded to the nearest 5-m (16-ft) interval. Other information recorded included whether or not the observation was auditory only and the 10-min interval of the 30-min survey in which the observation was initially noted.

## _Observation Schedule_

Sampling intensity was designed to document bird use and behavior by habitat and season within the study area. Surveys were conducted once per week during the summer (May 18 to

August 31), fall (September 1 to November 15), and winter (November 16 to February 28). Surveys were conducted during daylight hours and survey periods varied to approximately cover all daylight hours during a season. To the extent practical, each point was surveyed about the same number of times.

## _Incidental Wildlife Observations_

Incidental wildlife observations provide record of wildlife seen outside of the standardized surveys. All raptors, unusual or unique birds, sensitive species, mammals, amphibians, or reptiles were recorded. The observation number, date, time, species, number of individuals, sex/age class, distance from observer, activity, height above ground (for bird species), habitat, and, in the case of sensitive species, the location was also recorded.

## **RESULTS**

This interim report presents the results of fixed-point bird use surveys conducted within the Project during the summer and fall of 2010 and the winter of 2010/2011, as well as incidental wildlife observations.

## **Fixed-Point Bird Use Surveys**

A total of 721 30-min fixed-point bird use surveys were conducted within Project during 41 visits from May 18, 2010, to February 28, 2011. A total of 288 fixed-point surveys were conducted in the summer during 16 visits, while 180 surveys were conducted in the fall during 10 visits, and 253 surveys were conducted in the winter during 15 visits.

Overall, 120 unique bird species were observed (Appendix A), and a total of 12,713 individual bird observations within 4,058 separate groups were recorded (Table 1, Appendix A). Passerines were the most abundant bird type observed, accounting for 71.3% of all observations. This was primarily due to relatively high numbers of horned lark ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ; 1,904 observations), dark-eyed junco ( _Junco hyemali_ s; 1,406), white-crowned sparrow ( _Zonotrichia leucophrys_ ; 753), western scrub-jay ( _Aphelocoma californica_ ; 715), and mountain bluebird ( _Sialia currucoides_ ; 656; Appendix A). These five passerine species represented only 4.2% of all species observed, yet they accounted for 42.7% of the total bird observations. Large corvids were the second most abundant bird type observed in the study area, representing 12.0% of all observations, and common raven ( _Corvus corax_ ; 1,522 individuals) was the most common large corvid species observed during the surveys. Upland game birds were the third most abundant bird type observed, accounting for 9.7% of all observations. This was primarily due to relatively high numbers of California quail ( _Callipepla californica_ ; 860 individual observations) and chukar ( _Alectoris chukar_ ; 368; Appendix A).

A total of 269 diurnal raptor observations were made during fixed-point surveys (Table 1), representing 10 distinct species (Appendix A). Diurnal raptors accounted for 2.1% of all observations, with red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ), American kestrel ( _Falco sparverius_ ), and golden eagle ( _Aquila chrysaetos)_ being the most commonly observed diurnal raptors (118, 67, and 26 observations, respectively; Appendix A). Other raptors observed regularly during surveys included prairie falcon ( _Falco mexicanus_ ; 18 observations), Cooper’s hawk ( _Accipiter cooperii_ ; 14), and sharp-shinned hawk ( _Accipiter striatus_ ; 13). Two species of owl (great horned owl [ _Bubo virginianus_ ; two observations] and western screech owl [ _Megascops kennicottii_ ; one] and one species of vulture (turkey vulture [ _Cathartes aura_ ; 15 groups totaling 155 individual observations]) were also observed during surveys.

Eleven bird species were observed incidentally during the study, totaling 60 observations within 38 separate groups (Table 2). Golden eagle (18 observations) was the most commonly recorded incidental observation. Two species, American white pelican ( _Pelecanus erythrorhynchos_ ; one group comprising 14 individuals) and Swainson’s hawk ( _Buteo swainsoni_ ; one individual), were recorded only as incidental observations (i.e., these species were not observed during standardized surveys). Three mammal species, black-tailed jackrabbit ( _Lepus californicus_ ; three observations), black bear ( _Ursus americana_ ; one) and bobcat ( _Lynx rufus_ ; one), were also observed incidentally at the Project.

## _Sensitive Species_

One state-endangered species (CDFG 2010), willow flycatcher ( _Empidonax trailii_ ; five observations), and six state species of special concern (CDFG 2011) were observed during fixed-point surveys (Table 3, Figure 2). The six state species of special concern (CDFG 2011) included: loggerhead shrike ( _Lanius ludovicianus_ ; 83 observations), Vaux’s swift ( _Chaetura vauxi_ ; 44), American white pelican ( _Pelecanus erythrorhynchos_ ; 14), northern harrier (two individuals), gray vireo ( _Vireo vicinior_ ; one), and yellow warbler ( _Dendroica petechia_ ; one). The loggerhead shrike is also a federal species of concern (USFWS 2008). Ferruginous hawk (three observations), a federal species of concern (USFWS 2008) and a federal regionally-threatened species (USFWS 2011) was also recorded during surveys. Additionally, 26 golden eagles were recorded during surveys (Table 3). While not a federal or state species of concern, the golden eagle is legally protected under the federal Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (BGEPA 1940), and is a fully protected species in California (CDFG 2011).

## **DISCUSSION**

The studies implemented at the Project during the summer and fall of 2010 and winter of 2010/2011 are part of a larger 1-year study. Seasonal interim reports are designed to give CH2M HILL an early warning if high wildlife use is documented during surveys or if sensitive species are observed.

## **Bird Use Surveys**

Species diversity of birds observed during fixed-point surveys generally reflected the Mojavean woodland and scrub habitats comprising the majority of the study area. Resident breeding birds of dry, open, juniper woodlands were dominant, with species such as California quail, California towhee ( _Pipilo crissalis_ ), lark sparrow ( _Chondestes grammacus_ ), oak titmouse ( _Baeolophus inornatus_ ), rock wren ( _Salpinctes obsoletus_ ), sage sparrow (Amphispiza belli), and western scrub-jay commonly observed throughout the summer. A number of species were observed primarily during late May/early June or during the fall, indicating use of the area by migrants (e.g., lesser goldfinch [ _Carduelis psaltria_ ], mountain bluebird, pine siskin [ _Carduelis pinus_ ], rubycrowned kinglet [ _Regulus calendula_ ], yellow-rumped warbler [ _Dendroica coronatra_ ], Vaux’s swift, and willow flycatcher). During the winter surveys, species diversity declined but the overall number of observations increased. About 44% percent of the total bird observations were made during the winter, with year-round residents or wintering species, such as turkey vulture, common raven, dark-eyed junco, horned lark, mountain bluebird, western bluebird ( _Sialia mexicana_ ), and white-crowned sparrow, observed in relatively large numbers during this season.

Raptors were observed regularly throughout the summer, fall, and winter, with red-tailed hawk and American kestrel being the most commonly observed raptor species, composing 68.8% of the diurnal raptor observations. Other raptor species observed consistently throughout all three seasons included Cooper’s hawk, golden eagle, and prairie falcon. The majority (58.6%) of accipiters were observed during the fall, while buteos were most common during summer and winter, and falcons were most common during summer (Table 1, Appendix A).

## **Sensitive Species**

One state-endangered species (willow flycatcher; CDFG 2010), and six state species of special concern (loggerhead shrike, Vaux’s swift, American white pelican, gray vireo, northern harrier, and yellow warbler; CDFG 2011) were observed during the fixed-point surveys (Appendix A). A federal species of concern loggerhead shrike, and a federal species of concern and a regionally threatened species, ferruginous hawk (USFWS 2008, 2011), were also recorded during surveys (Appendix A), as well as golden eagle, which is legally protected under the federal BGEPA (1940), and is a fully protected species in California (CDFG 2011). Sensitive species recorded only as incidental observations at the Project included the state-threatened Swainson’s hawk (CDFG 2010) and a state species of special concern, American white pelican (CDFG 2011; Table 3). Golden eagles, ferruginous hawks, and northern harriers were also observed

incidentally to the fixed-point surveys. Use by these species is not unexpected given the general Project location.

## **Comparison of Seasonal Raptor Use**

Diurnal raptors have received much attention due to comparatively high rates of fatalities at the Altamont Pass wind energy facility in California, which has the highest recorded overall raptor fatality rate of any wind energy facility (Erickson et al. 2002b). Based on the results from other wind resource areas, the adjusted mean raptor use (number of raptors divided by the number of 800-m plots and the total number of surveys) in the Project was low during the summer, fall, and winter (0.25, 0.27, and 0.20 raptors/plot/20-min survey, respectively) relative to data collected at other existing and proposed wind energy facilities with similarly collected data for summer, fall, or winter seasons (Figures 3, 4, and 5).
